title: Varicocele
intro: A varicocele is a swelling of the veins within the scrotum, similar to varicose veins in the legs. It is common, usually on the left side, and often causes no problems. Sometimes it causes discomfort or is linked with reduced fertility, and treatment is considered in those cases.

sections.heading: What it is
paragraphs: Veins that drain blood from the testicle have valves. When valves fail, blood pools and the veins widen, forming a soft lump often described as feeling like a bag of worms. The swelling is more visible when standing and may shrink when lying down. It usually appears in adolescence or young adulthood.

sections.heading: Symptoms
paragraphs: Many men notice no symptoms. Others have a dull ache or heaviness, which is worse after standing for a long time or exercise and eases when lying down, a visible or palpable swelling or a smaller testicle on the affected side. Sudden onset in an older man or a varicocele that does not empty when lying down needs to be checked, as rarely it can be caused by a growth.

sections.heading: Diagnosis
paragraphs: A doctor examines the scrotum while you stand and lie down, sometimes with a cough or strain test, and often uses ultrasound to confirm and exclude other causes. If fertility is a concern, a semen analysis is performed. In adolescents, testicular size is monitored.

sections.heading: Treatment
paragraphs: Treatment is not needed if there are no symptoms and fertility is normal. Pain can be treated with supportive underwear and painkillers. Procedures to close the vein are offered for persistent pain, a clearly smaller testicle in a teenager, or abnormal semen results with fertility goals. Options include keyhole or microsurgical surgery and embolisation through a catheter. Risks include fluid collection around the testicle, recurrence and, rarely, testicular damage.

sections.heading: Varicocele and fertility
paragraphs: Varicoceles are found in many men with infertility, but also in many fertile men. Repair may improve semen quality in some, though the effect on pregnancy rates is uncertain and depends on the couple's situation. Discuss the options, including assisted reproduction, with a specialist.

examples.title: Seeking assessment
examples.text: Imagine you notice a soft swelling that is more visible when standing. You could arrange an examination and ask whether an ultrasound is needed.

examples.title: Considering fertility
examples.text: Suppose you and your partner have been trying for a child for a year. You might ask for a semen analysis and discuss whether repair would help.
